correctness.rationale: For a pure-block boundary point ιj y, convexity and the one-sided derivative of Σ||xj+tvj|| imply strict dominance ||vj||>Σk≠j||vk|| whenever a global direction illuminates it. The strict dominance cones are disjoint, and projection of any ordinary or fractional illuminating family from each such cone gives the factor lower bounds. Conversely extend factor directions by zero outside their block; at a boundary point with some nonzero coordinate, any direction illuminating its normalized factor boundary point illuminates the entire free sum. Fractional infima pass via arbitrary finite ε-approximation. For Euclidean balls, open hemispheres require d+1 directions, and uniform integration gives the sharp fractional lower bound 2; finite spherical partition approximants approach mass 2. The argument explicitly treats dimension one and r=1, strict tangent directions, and Borel-versus-finite weights. No numerical experiments are required or presented as proof.
residual_risks: The exact fractional value for smooth Euclidean factors need not be attained by a finite family, and is stated as infimum.

value.rationale: The all-factors equality is a motivated structural calculus for a fundamental convex-body operation. It gives sharp ordinary and fractional numbers for many nonsmooth norm balls and explains linear rather than product/exponential scaling; the exact identities for arbitrary factors are useful independently of future theorems.
residual_risks: Finite-dimensional central symmetry and ℓ1-sum geometry are essential; no claim about products or p>1.

final_claim: For arbitrary finite nonzero real normed spaces with unit balls Bj, illumination of their ℓ1/free-sum ball satisfies I(B)=ΣI(Bj) and I*(B)=ΣI*(Bj); for real Euclidean factor dimensions dj this is I=Σdj+r, I*=2r, hence complex ℓ1 ball in C^r has I=3r and I*=2r.
